query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing an in‐situ interlayer thermal management strategy via adjusted laser remelting with controlled preheat during additive manufacturing will reduce thermal gradients, minimize solidification shrinkage and porosity, and thereby improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity of high-entropy-alloy components.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy parts produced by conventional LPBF without active thermal management, which typically exhibit higher thermal gradients leading to dimensional inaccuracies, defects (e.g., porosity and hot cracks), and compromised mechanical properties.
generation.intervention: Integrate an in‐situ interlayer thermal management approach that employs adjusted laser remelting with controlled preheat by optimizing laser scan parameters in conjunction with active build plate temperature control.
generation.conditions: This intervention is applied during the laser powder bed fusion process under ambient atmosphere with optimized laser energy settings and preheat levels tailored for HEA fabrication.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduction in thermal gradients between layers that minimizes residual stresses, solidification shrinkage, and porosity.
generation.mechanism: Controlled preheating and remelting homogenize layer temperatures, which decreases thermal stress and prevents localized overheating during layer deposition. This leads to finer, more uniform microstructures with fewer defects and improved mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the conventional LPBF baseline, the intervention is predicted to significantly reduce fabrication-induced defects while enhancing dimensional precision and mechanical properties such as yield strength and ductility. However, the exact magnitude of improvement may depend on specific process conditions.
generation.baseline: Standard additive manufacturing of HEA components without active thermal management, which often results in higher defect density, dimensional inaccuracies, and suboptimal mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The benefits of this approach are expected to hold for HEA components fabricated under controlled ambient conditions with standardized part geometries; however, its effectiveness might diminish in extremely complex geometries or when scaling to very large builds.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains in quantifying the specific improvement levels across different HEA compositions and geometries. Further optimization and parameter tuning may be necessary, and the robustness of the approach across varying processing scales is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of HEA components using LPBF: one set using the standard process and one set with the in‐situ interlayer thermal management intervention (adjusted laser remelting with controlled preheat). All other processing parameters (laser power, scan speed, layer thickness) are held constant. The samples will then undergo comparative analysis.
measurements: Dimensional precision using coordinate measuring machines or 3D scanning
Defect density (porosity, hot cracking) evaluated via micro-CT or metallography
Mechanical properties (yield strength, tensile strength, ductility) assessed through tensile testing
Microstructural analysis via SEM to quantify grain size and defect distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples produced with the thermal management intervention do not show statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision, reduced defect density, and enhanced mechanical integrity compared to the baseline samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Manufacturing processes have a strong influence on the mechanical properties of HEAs. It has been determined that the CoCrFeNi part produced by the hot-rolling process has a better yield and ultimate strength compared to the casted parts [,,,]. Additive manufacturing processes, such as Laser-Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), can improve the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys due to their inherent unique processing characteristics. Specifically, the rapid solidification and repeated remelting associated with these techniques facilitate the formation of fine grains and numerous substructures with a high density of dislocations, thereby enhancing the yield strength compared to conventionally processed alloys. Brif et al. [] showed that the yield strength of the CoCrFeNi alloy produced by the powder bed fusion (PBF) process is twice, respectively, the treble of that alloy in as-cast condition, and Kuzminova [] showed in turn that the yield strength of alloys using L-PBF is twice than that of hot-rolled alloys. However, the thermal cycling and partial remelting experienced by previous layers can significantly increase the hot cracking susceptibility of superalloys [].

One potential solution for the difficulties associated with RCCA development is to employ high-throughput fabrication techniques, such as 3D printing methods, in which localized melting of the material is achieved using lasers or electron beams [,,,,,,,,]. Laser-directed energy deposition (L-DED), a workhorse of additive manufacturing (AM), enables the rapid synthesis and evaluation of a wide range of compositional variants of complex alloy systems [,], potentially accelerating the material development process []. Because of the layer-by-layer deposition process, the chemical composition of each printed layer can be precisely controlled, thereby facilitating the fabrication of compositional gradients within a single part []. Moorehead et al. stated that AM could dramatically accelerate material development, potentially reducing the processing time by up to 100 times compared with traditional manufacturing methods []. AM of RCCAs can be achieved using either pre-alloyed powders or a blend of elemental powders. The latter option is particularly appealing because of its cost-effectiveness and powder quality. chosen.technique: adjusted laser remelting with controlled preheat implementation during the additive process
chosen.conditions: using optimized laser scan parameters combined with an active build plate temperature control strategy to achieve reduced thermal gradients during fabrication, thereby minimizing solidification shrinkage and porosity in HEA components
chosen.why: This intervention directly addresses the open question by targeting both dimensional precision and mechanical integrity. Prior studies often focused on either defect reduction or microstructural control in isolation. Here, by implementing an in‐situ thermal management step—via a controlled laser remelting and preheat regimen—the approach removes limitations of prior simplifications in thermal modeling. It leverages standard additive manufacturing experimental techniques to study how fine tuning the thermal profile can systematically reduce fabrication-induced defects, providing an opportunity to falsify the hypothesis if defects or dimensional imprecision persist despite controlled thermal conditions.
